statement: At a high school, $40\%$ of the students are in the upper grades and the rest are in the lower grades. Of the upper-grade students, $30\%$ ride a bike to school. Of the lower-grade students, $15\%$ ride a bike to school. A student who rides a bike to school is chosen at random. What is the probability that this student is in the upper grades?

choices.misconception: I multiplied $40\%$ by $30\%$ to get 0.12, which is the chance that a random student is an upper-grade bike rider, not the chance that a bike rider is in the upper grades.
I gave the percent of upper-grade students who ride a bike, $30\%$, which reverses the condition in the question.
I compared only the two bike percents, $\frac{30}{30 + 15}$, as if there were the same number of upper-grade and lower-grade students.

hints: Imagine the school has $1{,}000$ students. How many are in each group?
Count the bike riders in each group, then find what fraction of all bike riders are upper-grade students.
Out of $1{,}000$ students, $400$ are in the upper grades and $120$ of them ride a bike. Of the $600$ lower-grade students, $90$ ride a bike.

solutions.reliable: Suppose there are $1{,}000$ students. Then $400$ are upper-grade students, of whom $0.30(400) = 120$ bike, and $600$ are lower-grade students, of whom $0.15(600) = 90$ bike. There are $210$ bike riders, and $120$ of them are in the upper grades, so the probability is $\dfrac{120}{210} = \dfrac{4}{7}$.
solutions.elegant: As proportions of the whole school, upper-grade bike riders are $0.4 \cdot 0.3 = 0.12$ and lower-grade bike riders are $0.6 \cdot 0.15 = 0.09$, so the probability is $\dfrac{0.12}{0.12 + 0.09} = \dfrac{12}{21} = \dfrac{4}{7}$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
